# Plan a Week's Meals from What's Already in Your Fridge

> **In short:** You don't need a recipe app or a shopping list to plan a week of meals. Open the fridge, sort what you have into "use first" and "use later", then build a 7-day plan that uses the most perishable items first. About 30 minutes of work, no special tool required.

You stare into the fridge, see half a bag of carrots, two eggs, and some yoghurt that expires tomorrow, and feel that low-key dread of "what do I even make?" This guide turns that moment into a 30-minute plan. It's the same approach cooks and busy families use to cut waste and save money, and you can do it tonight with a pen and a piece of paper.

A quick note on date labels before we start. **Use-by** dates are about food safety — food past its use-by date may not be safe to eat, so use it or freeze it by that day. **Best-before** dates are about quality, not safety — food past its best-before date is often still perfectly fine to eat, just maybe not at its peak. When you read a label later in this guide, that's the difference.

## Before you start
- **Time:** about 30 minutes for the first plan, less once you get the hang of it.
- **Tools:** a pen and paper, or the notes app on your phone. Optional: your phone camera for a quick fridge photo.
- **Pantry check:** a quick look in the fridge, freezer, and pantry (the cupboard where you keep rice, pasta, tinned food, oils, and spices).
- **No app or account needed.** This is a hands-on method, not a software tutorial. If you'd like AI help later, any assistant (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat) can take your list and suggest recipes, but that's a separate step.

## Step 1 — Empty the fridge onto the counter
Take everything out of the fridge and place it on the kitchen counter, grouped by type: vegetables together, dairy together, meat or fish together, condiments and jars together. The point is to see what you actually own, not just what's visible through the door. What you'll see is a surprisingly large pile, often more than you expected. This is normal — most people underestimate their fridge by about a third. If it looks different on your counter (very small fridge, or a deep freezer), just work top-shelf down so nothing hides.
💬 Example: pull out the cheese drawer, the veg crisper, and the little door shelves too. A 5-minute job.
You'll know it worked when every shelf is empty and you can see the back wall of the fridge.

## Step 2 — Sort into "use first" and "use later"
Make two piles on the counter. **Use first** is anything that will go off in the next 3 days: soft vegetables, opened milk, fresh meat or fish, ripe fruit, leftover containers. **Use later** is hardier stuff: carrots, potatoes, onions, whole eggs, unopened packs, jars, anything from the freezer. Don't throw anything away yet — sorting first helps you decide what to cook, not what to bin. If a piece of meat smells off or vegetables are clearly slimy, set those aside in a small "compost" pile, but be honest: most "iffy" food is still fine to cook today. Remember the date-label note: use-by dates are the safety line, best-before is only about quality.
💬 Example: a half-empty milk carton with a 2-day use-by date goes in "use first". A sealed jar of pickles goes in "use later".
You'll know it worked when each item on the counter sits in exactly one pile, and the "use first" pile is the smaller one.

## Step 3 — Check the pantry and freezer too
Spend 2 minutes looking at the dry pantry and the freezer. Write down — or take a phone photo of — anything you might forget: rice, pasta, tinned tomatoes, lentils, frozen peas, frozen bread, leftover roast chicken. Think of this as your "supporting cast". The fridge gives you the stars; the pantry and freezer give you the carb, the protein backup, and the speed. If your freezer is packed with mystery bags, label them right now with a sticky note ("beef, March 2026") so future-you isn't guessing.
💬 Example: "We have basmati rice, two tins of tomatoes, a bag of frozen peas, and half a loaf of bread in the freezer."
You'll know it worked when you have a short list of staples you can mix with anything from the fridge.

## Step 4 — Pick one "anchor" meal per day
For the next 7 days, give each day one anchor meal that uses up the most perishable ingredients. Spread the fresh meat, fish, and soft vegetables across the week so nothing sits past its prime. The other meals can be simple repeats: breakfasts are usually the same 2–3 things, lunches are often leftovers from dinner, and one or two nights a week can be a "pantry meal" (pasta, omelette, fried rice) that doesn't need any fresh shopping.
💬 Example week: Monday stir-fry (uses the soft capsicum and half the chicken), Wednesday frittata (uses the eggs and any leftover veg), Friday curry (uses the sad carrots and a tin of lentils), with toast, yoghurt, and leftovers filling the gaps.
You'll know it worked when you can glance at the plan and see that nothing in the "use first" pile is left unassigned by Day 3.

## Step 5 — Write the plan in a simple grid
On a piece of paper, draw 7 columns (one per day) and 3 rows (breakfast, lunch, dinner). Fill in each box with one short phrase — not a recipe, just a name. "Eggs on toast", "leftover curry", "pasta with peas and parmesan". The whole plan should fit on one side of an A4 page. If a box is hard to fill, swap two days around so the most perishable food gets cooked earliest. If it looks different on your phone (you prefer digital notes), use a notes app with a simple table — the shape is the same.
💬 Example: "Tues lunch: last night's chicken + salad leaves. Sat dinner: pantry fried rice (rice, egg, frozen peas, soy sauce)."
You'll know it worked when you can read the plan in under 30 seconds and know exactly what to take out of the fridge each morning.

## Step 6 — Shop only for the gaps
Now look at your plan and make a short shopping list — only for things you genuinely need to make it work. Common gaps: fresh bread, milk, one or two vegetables, maybe a protein. Most weeks you'll find you need almost nothing. Stick to the list; this is the part that actually saves money. If you spot a gap you can't fill (you planned fish tacos but have no tortillas), change the plan, not the shopping list — swap the meal for something that uses what you already have.
💬 Example list: "1 loaf bread, 1 L milk, 1 lettuce, 6 tortillas." That's it. Estimated cost: about $12.
You'll know it worked when your shopping basket is noticeably lighter than usual and you haven't bought anything random.

## Step 7 — Cook once, eat twice
Pick one evening — usually Sunday or your day off — to cook a slightly larger portion, and box the leftovers for a lunch or a quick dinner later in the week. This is the single biggest time-saver in weekly cooking, and it turns "leftovers" from a chore into the plan. Cooked rice, cooked pasta, roast vegetables, and soups all keep 3–4 days in the fridge and freeze well. If it looks different on your schedule (you work long hours), don't skip this step — instead, cook a double batch on any evening you already have the oven or stove on.
💬 Example: while the curry is simmering, boil an extra cup of rice. Tomorrow's lunch is sorted in 30 seconds.
You'll know it worked when at least 2 lunches and 1 dinner this week come straight from the fridge without any new cooking.

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake:** Throwing away "iffy" food before checking. **Fix:** Smell it, look at it, and remember that best-before is a quality date, not a safety date for most things. Use-by is the safety date — respect it, but food past best-before is usually still fine if it looks and smells normal. Soft vegetables and slightly tired herbs are usually fine if cooked today.
- **Mistake:** Planning 7 ambitious recipes. **Fix:** Cap it at 2 or 3 new dishes per week. The rest should be simple repeats, leftovers, or pantry meals. A plan you don't cook is not a plan.
- **Mistake:** Shopping before planning. **Fix:** Always plan from the fridge first, then write the shopping list. If you shop first, you'll overbuy and the plan stops mattering.
- **Mistake:** Forgetting breakfasts and lunches. **Fix:** Most plans fail because dinner gets all the attention. Give breakfast one default (eggs, oats, toast) and let lunch be leftovers twice a week.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** food waste is a real cost. American government and waste-reduction reports (such as those from Foodbank and Fight Food Waste the US) regularly find that many households throw out a meaningful share of the food they buy — often around one-fifth of the weekly shop. A fridge-first plan usually shrinks that quickly, often by half or more within a month of starting. The exact dollar saving depends on your household size and shopping habits, but reducing waste is the most reliable way to put money back in the food budget.
- **For your business or work:** the same "use what you have first" logic works for office lunches, shared kitchen snacks, and even team lunches. Cook once on Sunday, eat well all week, and avoid the 4pm takeaway trap.
- **If you're just getting started:** do this just for dinners this week. Skip breakfast and lunch planning entirely. Once dinners feel easy, add the rest.

## Try it now
Pick one shelf of your fridge — just one — and plan three dinners from what's on it. Not the whole fridge, not the whole week. Just one shelf, three nights, shopping list of nothing. That single small win is how fridge-first planning actually becomes a habit.
